title: Postmortem: Payment API Connection Pool Starvation During Flash Sale
timeline:
14:20 Peak traffic began (1400 req/s)
14:22 QueuePool limit reached, HTTP 500 error rate surged to 42%
14:25 SRE triggered diagnostic check on active DB connections
14:28 Restart of payment-api service executed to clear hung socket handles
14:30 Connection pool capacity increased from 30 to 50
14:34 Error rate dropped to 0.1%, incident closed.
root_cause: The maximum connection pool size was set to 20 with 10 overflow connections. Slow analytical queries from the checkout transaction logger occupied pool connections, causing checkout API requests to wait and time out.
contributing_factors:
1. Analytics queries executed in the primary transactional connection pool.
2. Lack of proactive connection pool utilization alerting before reaching 90% threshold.
3. Short connection timeout (30s) under high concurrency.
resolution: Restarted payment-api service instances to terminate hung connections, followed by scaling pool capacity to 50 and routing analytical queries to read-replica pool.
what_worked: Service restart rapidly flushed hung sockets. Vector search quickly identified previous connection starvation runbook.
what_failed: Automated alerting fired 4 minutes after error rate spiked instead of alerting on pool queue saturation.
preventive_actions:
1. Separate read-only analytical queries into dedicated replica pool.
2. Add Prometheus alert at 75% connection pool utilization.
3. Implement exponential backoff on DB connection retries.
lessons_learned: Never mix heavy read workloads with critical checkout transaction threads on shared connection pools.

title: Postmortem: Auth Service JWT Key Rotation Desync Outage
timeline:
09:00 Scheduled automated JWT key rotation completed
09:01 Influx of 401 Unauthorized errors across all microservices
09:03 SRE discovered JWKS cache in Redis was still serving stale public keys
09:05 JWKS cache purged and auth-service restarted
09:08 Verification passed, 401 errors ceased.
root_cause: JWKS public key cache TTL was hardcoded to 86400 seconds (24h) without an invalidation webhook handler upon key rotation.
contributing_factors: Key rotation ran in production without a pre-flight canary test of JWKS cache invalidation.
resolution: Flushed Redis JWKS cache and restarted auth-service pods to fetch the latest public key.
what_worked: Rolling restart of auth service immediately refreshed the public key cache.
what_failed: Downstream services had no fallback grace period for previous public key.
preventive_actions:
1. Add cache-busting pub/sub event to key rotation job.
2. Support overlapping dual-key signing window for 48 hours.
lessons_learned: Crypto key rotation must always support N-1 key overlap and proactive cache invalidation.

title: Postmortem: Order Service OOM Crash Loop on Large Batch Export
timeline:
23:45 End-of-day invoice generation cron triggered
23:46 Order-service container memory breached 1024MB limit, OOMKilled by Linux kernel
23:48 Kubernetes restarted pod, which crashed again upon resuming batch
23:52 Rollback to v3.1.1 executed, temporarily bumping container memory to 2048MB
23:57 Pod stabilized, batch completed successfully.
root_cause: A new query optimization in v3.1.2 removed SQL cursor pagination, causing the batch exporter to load 450,000 JSON records into single memory array.
contributing_factors: Unit tests were only run against mock datasets of 50 records.
resolution: Rolled back to v3.1.1 and temporarily doubled container memory allocation.
what_worked: Deployment rollback stopped the crash-loop instantly.
what_failed: Memory limit was set too tight without OOM headroom alerting.
preventive_actions:
1. Enforce cursor streaming for all batch operations.
2. Add memory stress testing to CI/CD pipeline.
lessons_learned: Data exports must always stream chunks rather than buffering unconstrained datasets in memory.

title: Postmortem: Postgres Table Lock Deadlock During Flash Inventory Decrement
timeline:
11:15 Flash sale began with 200 concurrent multi-item cart checkouts
11:16 Postgres reported deadlock detected between TX_91283 and TX_91290
11:19 Lock wait queue accumulated 42 blocked connections
11:23 Terminated blocking backend PIDs and restarted connection proxy
11:33 Lock contention cleared, normal latency restored.
root_cause: Multiple inventory item deductions acquired row locks in arbitrary client cart order rather than sorting SKU IDs before locking.
contributing_factors: High volume of multi-item carts during flash sale caused cyclic lock dependencies.
resolution: Terminated blocking queries and deployed fix to enforce ordered SKU locking in application SQL queries.
what_worked: Terminating long-running blocking query PIDs broke the circular wait chain.
what_failed: No automated lock timeout threshold was configured in Postgres.
preventive_actions:
1. Always sort lock targets by primary key before acquiring exclusive locks.
2. Set statement_timeout and lock_timeout in PostgreSQL.
lessons_learned: Circular deadlocks can be mathematically eliminated by enforcing consistent lock acquisition ordering.

title: Postmortem: User Service Session Cache Thundering Herd
timeline:
16:10 Redis reached 4096MB maxmemory limit and triggered key eviction
16:11 Active user sessions were evicted, forcing 50,000 requests directly to primary DB
16:13 Database CPU spiked to 98%, request timeouts cascaded
16:16 Purged non-essential telemetry cache keys and restarted user-service connection pool
16:25 DB CPU returned to 14%, cache hit ratio recovered to 96%.
root_cause: Telemetry debug payloads were saved into the same Redis instance as session tokens without an explicit TTL, exhausting RAM.
contributing_factors: Lack of separate Redis clusters for ephemeral telemetry vs critical session authentication.
resolution: Purged telemetry cache namespace and restarted user-service cache connection pool.
what_worked: Cache namespace cleanup and connection pool restart freed 2.2GB of Redis RAM.
what_failed: Cache eviction policy was set to volatile-lru instead of allkeys-lru with alerts.
preventive_actions:
1. Isolate telemetry logs from Redis session storage.
2. Set strict TTLs on all cache writes.
lessons_learned: Never mix high-throughput telemetry data with critical auth session caches on single Redis clusters.

title: Postmortem: Payment API Synchronous Webhook Timeout Cascade
timeline:
08:33 Stripe webhook callbacks spiked after banking batch settlement
08:34 Fraud check microservice became sluggish, causing webhook handlers to hit 30s timeout
08:36 Payment gateway began retrying timed-out webhooks, creating a 504 storm
08:40 Enabled asynchronous webhook queue mode and restarted worker pool
08:44 Webhook response time dropped from 30s to 45ms.
root_cause: Webhook handler performed synchronous HTTP calls to fraud and billing services within the inbound HTTP request thread.
contributing_factors: Third-party fraud scoring API experienced intermittent degradation.
resolution: Switched payment webhook ingestion to asynchronous queue model and restarted payment-api worker pool.
what_worked: Decoupling webhook ingestion into message queue restored immediate 200 OK acknowledgments.
what_failed: Synchronous coupling created severe backpressure on webhook ingress gateway.
preventive_actions:
1. Ingest webhooks into RabbitMQ/SQS immediately and acknowledge 200 OK within 50ms.
2. Process fraud evaluation in background workers.
lessons_learned: External webhooks must always be acknowledged immediately and processed asynchronously.

title: Postmortem: Cloudflare Trusted Proxy IP Misconfiguration
timeline:
13:40 Ingress configuration update deployed
13:41 Legitimate users worldwide received 429 Too Many Requests on login
13:44 SRE identified that rate limiter was grouping all traffic under single proxy IP 10.0.0.1
13:46 Updated trusted proxy header configuration and restarted auth-service
13:49 429 errors dropped to 0%, normal login restored.
root_cause: The reverse proxy trust header configuration was omitted in deployment config, causing rate limiter middleware to use socket IP instead of CF-Connecting-IP.
contributing_factors: Staging environment was not behind Cloudflare proxy, so rate limiting tests passed in QA.
resolution: Restored CF-Connecting-IP header evaluation and restarted auth-service.
what_worked: Fast service restart applied updated proxy trust configuration in under 3 minutes.
what_failed: QA environment lacked parity with production CDN proxy topology.
preventive_actions:
1. Add automated CDN header validation to staging test suites.
2. Alert when single IP account for >10% of total rate limiter blocks.
lessons_learned: Rate limiting middleware must strictly validate forwarded client headers in all environments.

title: Postmortem: Kafka Consumer Rebalance Storm on Heavy PDF Generation
timeline:
17:15 End-of-month PDF receipt generation surge began
17:17 Consumer thread spent 45s generating complex invoice, exceeding max.poll.interval.ms (30s)
17:18 Kafka coordinator deemed consumer dead and triggered group rebalance
17:21 Rebalance loop prevented all partitions from committing offsets
17:25 Increased poll interval to 180s and performed rolling restart of order-service
17:31 Consumer group stabilized and lag drained.
root_cause: Single-threaded synchronous PDF generation blocked the consumer event loop beyond the Kafka heartbeat poll interval.
contributing_factors: max.poll.interval.ms was set to default 30000ms which was too short for large invoice generation.
resolution: Increased max.poll.interval.ms to 180s and restarted order-service consumer group.
what_worked: Increasing poll interval and restarting consumer group allowed consumers to process heavy messages without triggering rebalances.
what_failed: Heavy computation was run directly inside message polling loop.
preventive_actions:
1. Offload heavy PDF generation to dedicated worker thread pool.
2. Keep Kafka consumer polling thread strictly dedicated to ingestion.
lessons_learned: Never execute blocking CPU-heavy tasks inside Kafka consumer poll loops.

title: Postmortem: Postgres WAL Disk Exhaustion Outage
timeline:
04:12 S3 backup bucket permissions expired due to IAM policy change
04:15 Postgres WAL archiver failed to offload logs to S3, causing WAL segments to pile up on local disk
04:18 Disk utilization reached 99.8%, Postgres automatically transitioned to read-only panic state
04:24 IAM role restored, WAL archiver restarted, old logs cleared
04:34 Postgres returned to healthy read-write state.
root_cause: PostgreSQL accumulated unarchived WAL segments on local disk when S3 archival backup failed due to an expired IAM role.
contributing_factors: Disk space alerting threshold was set to 95%, leaving only 5 minutes of buffer during high transaction rate.
resolution: Fixed IAM policy, restarted WAL archiver background process, and expanded disk capacity to 250GB.
what_worked: Postgres fail-safe read-only mode prevented database corruption.
what_failed: WAL archival failure alert was missing in Datadog.
preventive_actions:
1. Add alert on pg_stat_archiver failed_count > 0.
2. Implement disk auto-scaling for database volumes.
lessons_learned: Database archiver health is as critical as query performance; monitor WAL backlog continuously.

title: Postmortem: Payment Webhook HMAC Verification Failure Post-Release
timeline:
15:30 Deployment v2.2.4 released to production
15:31 100% of incoming payment webhooks rejected with 400 Bad Request
15:34 SRE discovered new logging middleware altered request body before HMAC hash calculation
15:37 Executed rollback_deployment to v2.2.3
15:40 Webhook verification rate returned to 100%, missed callbacks retried.
root_cause: Logging middleware in v2.2.4 parsed and re-serialized JSON payload, altering whitespace and invalidating cryptographic HMAC signature.
contributing_factors: Webhook HMAC verification was mocked in integration tests rather than tested with raw binary payloads.
resolution: Rolled back to v2.2.3 and updated middleware to preserve raw request stream.
what_worked: Deployment rollback to v2.2.3 restored system functionality in 3 minutes.
what_failed: Integration tests did not test raw bytes HMAC signature verification.
preventive_actions:
1. Use raw unmodified body stream for all cryptographic signature checks.
2. Add end-to-end webhook replay tests in staging.
lessons_learned: Cryptographic signatures depend on exact byte representation; never let JSON parsers mutate raw request bodies.
